families.s: HSE cleaning-industry slip, chemical, equipment and ergonomic guidance
families.t: wet floors, trailing cables, chemical assessment, equipment selection, segregation, communication, maintenance, manual work and work at height
f: Cleaning work can create slip and trip hazards through wet floors and trailing equipment cables.
Employers must assess and control risks to cleaners and other people entering the area.
The cleaning method and chemical should be suitable for the contaminant and floor surface.
Cleaning equipment must be maintained so it remains effective and does not introduce additional hazards.
Work should be planned to segregate wet areas or warn and control access until the floor is safe.
Cleaning chemicals require COSHH assessment, safe dilution, storage, instruction and suitable PPE where needed.
Cleaning-sector risks also include skin disease, back pain, work at height and window-cleaning hazards.
Communication between employers, cleaners, building users and equipment or chemical suppliers is important.
families.g: Cleaning risk depends on floor and contamination, method, chemical, dilution, equipment condition, timing, access control, worker posture, height and communication.

families.s: HSE catering and hospitality workplace-safety guidance
families.t: risk assessment, knives, gas appliances, cooking fumes, cleaning chemicals, slips, hot equipment and young-worker restrictions
f: Catering and hospitality employers must assess and manage workplace health and safety risks.
Knives should be suitable for the task, maintained and used under safe systems of work.
Gas appliances, flues, pipework and safety devices must be maintained in a safe condition.
Cooking fumes can contain oil mist, smoke, irritants and carbon monoxide from gas-fired equipment.
Cleaning chemicals and some food ingredients can cause dermatitis, skin allergy or asthma.
Spillages, cleaning and busy routes create significant slip risks that require prompt control.
Hot liquids, fryers, ovens, steam and heated surfaces require safe handling and guarding arrangements.
Young workers may need to be prohibited from high-risk tasks such as slicers, compactors, corrosive chemicals, fryer draining and work at height.
families.g: Catering risk depends on menu and processes, heat and gas equipment, ventilation, knives and machinery, cleaning chemicals, floor contamination, pace, staffing, competence and worker age.

families.s: HSE fairground and amusement-device design, inspection and operation guidance
families.t: controller and operator duties, design review, inspection, maintenance, pre-use checks, public protection, children and impaired users
f: Fairground controllers and operators have duties to keep amusement devices safe for workers and the public.
Safe practice covers design, manufacture, installation, operation, maintenance, inspection and modification.
Controllers should use competent inspection bodies and recognised inspection arrangements.
Required documentation and inspection evidence should be available before public operation.
Operators should complete pre-use checks and follow operating limits and instructions.
Defects affecting safety require the device to be taken out of use until corrected.
Public controls should address barriers, loading, restraint, behaviour and emergency arrangements.
Children and people affected by alcohol, drugs or other limitations may require additional operating controls.
families.g: Ride risk depends on device design and history, inspection, maintenance, setup, loading, restraints, weather, operator competence, user behaviour, crowd control and emergency response.

families.s: HSE bouncy-castle and inflatable-play-equipment safety guidance
families.t: commercial supply, anchorage, wind, blowers, pressure, inspection, supervision, user limits and shutdown
f: Health and safety law applies to the commercial supply, hire and use of inflatable play equipment.
Serious incidents have occurred when inflatables collapsed or were blown away in windy conditions.
The inflatable must be installed using the specified anchorage system on suitable ground.
Blowers, air tubes and electrical supplies should be protected and checked before use.
Wind and weather conditions must be monitored and the equipment shut down at the applicable limit.
Operation requires active supervision and enforcement of user numbers, size and behaviour limits.
Competent annual inspection or an equivalent recognised scheme provides evidence of condition.
Users should be kept away from walls, anchor points, blowers and other prohibited areas.
families.g: Inflatable-play risk depends on design, anchorage, ground, wind, blower and pressure, inspection, supervision, user size and number, electrical supply and emergency shutdown.

families.s: HSE sealed-inflatable supply, inspection, documentation and operation guidance
families.t: pressurised-air release, design review, initial test, operational compliance, pressure monitoring, maintenance manuals and operator controls
f: Sealed inflatables can create serious risks from uncontrolled or explosive release of pressurised air.
High winds can cause loss of control of some sealed inflatable devices.
Clear supplier, controller, inspection-body and operator roles are needed throughout the equipment lifecycle.
Essential evidence includes a design review and an initial physical test of the device.
A successful periodic thorough inspection should result in a Declaration of Operational Compliance or equivalent evidence.
The operations manual should include information needed for safe use, including internal-pressure measurement where relevant.
The maintenance manual should define inspection, maintenance and repair arrangements.
Operators should protect the base from abrasive or contaminated surfaces and enforce user restrictions stated by the manufacturer.
families.g: Sealed-inflatable risk depends on internal pressure, construction, age, inspection, repair, ground, weather, anchorage, operator controls, documentation and user activity.

families.s: HSE diacetyl-vapour exposure-control guidance for food and drink manufacture
families.t: heating, airborne concentration, workplace limits, substitution, enclosure, ventilation, monitoring, RPE and process control
f: Heating diacetyl can significantly increase airborne concentrations.
Inhalation exposure to diacetyl can cause serious respiratory disease.
Workplace exposure limits for diacetyl are listed in EH40.
Substitution or use of a less hazardous flavouring should be considered before relying on protective equipment.
Closed transfer, enclosure and local exhaust ventilation can reduce vapour release at source.
Process temperature and duration should be controlled to minimise volatilisation.
Exposure monitoring may be needed to verify that controls remain adequate.
Suitable RPE may be needed for residual risk, maintenance, cleaning or foreseeable abnormal releases.
families.g: Diacetyl risk depends on formulation, concentration, temperature, open handling, transfer, enclosure, ventilation, task duration, monitoring, maintenance and RPE.

families.s: HSE food-and-drink disinfectant exposure assessment and control guidance
families.t: chemical inventory, compatibility, dilution, spraying, substitution, ventilation, PPE, RPE, storage and emergency response
f: A disinfectant assessment should list the chemicals, their hazards and the measures used to control exposure.
Safe storage should account for chemical compatibility and prevent unintended mixing.
Working concentrations and dilution procedures should be defined and followed.
Application method and equipment should minimise inhalation and skin exposure.
Less hazardous formulations or non-spray application should be considered where practicable.
Ventilation or local extraction should control mist or vapour at source.
Suitable protective clothing, gloves, eye protection and RPE should be provided where the assessment requires them.
Spraying some aldehyde or peracetic-acid formulations can require airline breathing apparatus and full chemical protection.
families.g: Disinfectant risk depends on active ingredient, concentration, incompatibility, dilution, temperature, spray or foam method, ventilation, contact time, PPE, storage and spill response.

families.s: HSE chemical manufacture, supply, classification, storage and use guidance
families.t: UK REACH, GB CLP, SDS, inventory, compatibility, segregation, transport interfaces, COSHH and emergency planning
f: UK REACH applies to the majority of chemical substances manufactured in or imported into Great Britain.
GB CLP regulates classification, labelling and packaging of chemicals placed on the Great Britain market.
Manufacturers and suppliers must identify applicable duties before placing chemicals on the market.
Hazardous workplace chemicals should be supplied with the legally required safety data information.
Users must assess and control actual workplace risks under COSHH rather than relying only on the supply label.
Chemical activities can include manufacture, supply, storage, transport and use, each with distinct legal interfaces.
Storage arrangements should address compatibility, segregation, containment, inventory and access control.
Emergency planning should cover spills, fire, exposure, loss of containment and information for responders.
families.g: Chemical-supply risk depends on substance classification and quantity, process, packaging, compatibility, storage, transport, user information, inventory accuracy and emergency arrangements.
